77	## Motivation for Conditional Segment Initialization
78	
79	Under the current [threading proposal](https://github.com/WebAssembly/threads),
80	to share a module between multiple agents, the module must be instantiated
81	multiple times: once per agent. Instantiation initializes linear memory with
82	the contents in the module's data segments. If the memory is shared between
83	multiple agents, it will be initialized multiple times, potentially overwriting
84	stores that occurred after the previous initializations.
85	
86	For example:
87	
88	```webassembly
89	;; The module.
90	(module
91	  (memory (export "memory") 1)
92	
93	  ;; Some value used as a counter.
94	  (data (i32.const 0) "\0")
95	
96	  ;; Add one to the counter.
97	  (func (export "addOne")
98	    (i32.store8
99	      (i32.const 0)
100	      (i32.add
101	        (i32.load8_u (i32.const 0))
102	        (i32.const 1)))
103	  )
104	)
105	```
106	
107	```javascript
108	// main.js
109	let moduleBytes = ...;
110	
111	WebAssembly.instantiate(moduleBytes).then(
112	  ({module, instance}) => {
113	    // Increment our counter.
114	    instance.exports.addOne();
115	
116	    // Spawn a new Worker.
117	    let worker = new Worker('worker.js');
118	
119	    // Send the module to the new Worker.
120	    worker.postMessage(module);
121	  });
122	
123	// worker.js
124	
125	function onmessage(event) {
126	  let module = event.data;
127	
128	  // Use the module to create another instance.
129	  WebAssembly.instantiate(module).then(
130	    (instance) => {
131	      // Oops, our counter has been clobbered.
132	    });
133	}
134	
135	```
136	
137	This can be worked around by storing the data segments in a separate module
138	which is only instantiated once, then exporting this memory to be used by
139	another module that contains only code. This works, but it cumbersome since it
140	requires two modules where one should be enough.
141	
142	
143	## Motivation for combining Bulk Memory Operations + Conditional Segment Initialization Proposals
144	
145	When [discussing the design of Conditional Segment Initialization](https://github.com/WebAssembly/threads/issues/62),
146	we found that programmatic memory initialization from a read-only data segment
147	(via the `memory.init` instruction, described below) has similar behavior to the
148	proposed instruction to copy memory regions from linear memory (`memory.copy`,
149	also described below.)
150	
151	## Design
152	
153	Copying between regions in linear memory or a table is accomplished with the
154	new `*.copy` instructions:
155	
156	* `memory.copy`: copy from one region of linear memory to another
157	* `table.copy`: copy from one region of a table to another
158	
159	Filling a memory region can be accomplished with `memory.fill`:
160	
161	* `memory.fill`: fill a region of linear memory with a given byte value
162	
163	The [binary format for the data
164	section](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/binary/modules.html#binary-datasec)
165	currently has a collection of segments, each of which has a memory index, an
166	initializer expression for its offset, and its raw data.
167	
168	Since WebAssembly currently does not allow for multiple memories, the memory
169	index of each segment must be zero. We can repurpose this 32-bit integer as a
170	flags field where new meaning is attached to nonzero values.
171	
172	When the low bit of the new flags field is `1`, this segment is _passive_. A
173	passive segment will not be automatically copied into the memory or table on
174	instantiation, and must instead be applied manually using the following new
175	instructions:
176	
177	* `memory.init`: copy a region from a data segment
178	* `table.init`: copy a region from an element segment
179	
180	A passive segment has no initializer expression, since it will be specified
181	as an operand to `memory.init` or `table.init`.
182	
183	Segments can also be shrunk to size zero by using the following new instructions:
184	
185	* `data.drop`: discard the data in an data segment
186	* `elem.drop`: discard the data in an element segment
187	
188	An active segment is equivalent to a passive segment, but with an implicit
189	`memory.init` followed by a `data.drop` (or `table.init` followed by a
190	`elem.drop`) that is prepended to the module's start function.
191	
192	Additionally, the reference-types proposal introduces the notion of a function
193	reference (a function whose address is a program value).  To support this,
194	element segments can have several encodings, and can also be used to
195	forward-declare functions whose address will be taken; see below.
196	
197	The reference-types proposal also introduces the bulk instructions `table.fill`
198	and `table.grow`, both of which take a function reference as an initializer
199	argument.
200	
201	### Data segments
202	
203	The meaning of the bits of the flag field (a `varuint32`) for data segments is:
204	
205	| Bit | Meaning                                        |
206	| -   | -                                              |
207	| 0   | 0=is active, 1=is passive                      |
208	| 1   | if bit 0 clear: 0=memory 0, 1=has memory index |
209	
210	which yields this view, with the fields carried by each flag value:
211	
212	| Flags | Meaning                  | Memory index | Offset in memory | Count       | Payload |
213	| -     | -                        | -            | -                | -           | -       |
214	| 0     | Active                   |              | `init_expr`      | `varuint32` | `u8`*   |
215	| 1     | Passive                  |              |                  | `varuint32` | `u8`*   |
216	| 2     | Active with memory index | `varuint32`  | `init_expr`      | `varuint32` | `u8`*   |
217	
218	All other flag values are illegal.  At present the memory index must be zero,
219	but the upcoming multi-memory proposal changes that.
220	
221	
222	### Element segments
223	
224	The meaning of the bits of the flag field (a `varuint32`) for element segments is:
225	
226	| Bit | Meaning                                          |
227	| -   | -                                                |
228	| 0   | 0=is active, 1=is passive                        |
229	| 1   | if bit 0 clear: 0=table 0, 1=has table index     | 
230	|     | if bit 0 set: 0=active, 1=declared               |
231	| 2   | 0=carries indices; 1=carries elemexprs          |
232	
233	which yields this view, with the fields carried by each flag value:
234	
235	| Flag | Meaning                          | Table index | Offset in table | Encoding      | Count       | Payload      |
236	| -    | -                                | -           | -               | -             | -           | -            |
237	| 0    | Legacy active, funcref externval |             | `init_expr`     |               | `varuint32` | `idx`*       |
238	| 1    | Passive, externval               |             |                 | `extern_kind` | `varuint32` | `idx`*       |
239	| 2    | Active, externval                | `varuint32` | `init_expr`     | `extern_kind` | `varuint32` | `idx`*       |
240	| 3    | Declared, externval              |             |                 | `extern_kind` | `varuint32` | `idx`*       |
241	| 4    | Legacy active, funcref elemexpr  |             | `init_expr`     |               | `varuint32` | `elem_expr`* |
242	| 5    | Passive, elemexpr                |             |                 | `elem_type`   | `varuint32` | `elem_expr`* |
243	| 6    | Active, elemexpr                 | `varuint32` | `init_expr`     | `elem_type`   | `varuint32` | `elem_expr`* |
244	| 7    | Declared, elemexpr               |             |                 | `elem_type`   | `varuint32` | `elem_expr`* |
245	
246	All other flag values are illegal.  Note that the "declared" attribute
247	is not used by this proposal, but is used by the reference-types
248	proposal.
249	
250	The `extern_kind` must be zero, signifying a function definition.  An `idx` is a
251	`varuint32` that references an entity in the module, currently only its function
252	table.
253	
254	At present the table index must be zero, but the reference-types
255	proposal introduces a notion of multiple tables.
256	
257	An `elem_expr` is like an `init_expr`, but can only contain expressions of the following sequences:
258	
259	| Binary                | Text                    | Description                                |
260	| -                     | -                       | -                                          |
261	| `0xd0 0x0b`           | `ref.null end`          | Returns a null reference                   |
262	| `0xd2 varuint32 0x0b` | `ref.func $funcidx end` | Returns a reference to function `$funcidx` |
263	
264	### Segment Initialization
265	
266	In the MVP, segments are initialized during module instantiation. If any segment
267	would be initialized out-of-bounds, then the memory or table instance is not
268	modified.
269	
270	This behavior is changed in the bulk memory proposal:
271	
272	Each active segment is initialized in module-definition order. For
273	each segment, if reading the source or writing the destination would
274	go out of bounds, then instantiation fails at that point.  Data that
275	had already been written for previous (in-bounds) segments stays
276	written.
277	
278	### `memory.init` instruction
279	
280	The `memory.init` instruction copies data from a given passive segment into a target
281	memory. The target memory and source segment are given as immediates.
282	
283	The instruction has the signature `[i32 i32 i32] -> []`. The parameters are, in order:
284	
285	- top-2: destination address
286	- top-1: offset into the source segment
287	- top-0: size of memory region in bytes
288	
289	It is a validation error to use `memory.init` with an out-of-bounds segment index.
290	
291	A trap occurs if:
292	
293	* the source offset plus size is greater than the length of the source data segment;
294	  this includes the case that the segment has been dropped via `data.drop`
295	* the destination offset plus size is greater than the length of the target memory
296	
297	The order of writing is unspecified, though this is currently unobservable.
298	
299	Note that it is allowed to use `memory.init` on the same data segment more than
300	once.
301	
302	### `data.drop` instruction
303	
304	The `data.drop` instruction shrinks the size of the segment to zero. After a
305	data segment has been dropped, it can still be used in a `memory.init`
306	instruction, but only a zero-length access at offset zero will not trap.  This
307	instruction is intended to be used as an optimization hint to the WebAssembly
308	implementation. After a memory segment is dropped its data can no longer be
309	retrieved, so the memory used by this segment may be freed.
310	
311	It is a validation error to use `data.drop` with an out-of-bounds segment index.
312	
313	### `memory.copy` instruction
314	
315	Copy data from a source memory region to destination region.  The
316	regions are said to overlap if they are in the same memory and the
317	start address of one region is one of the addresses that's read or
318	written (by the copy operation) in the other region.
319	
320	This instruction has two immediate arguments: the source and
321	destination memory indices. They currently both must be zero.
322	
323	Copying takes place as if an intermediate buffer were used, allowing the
324	destination and source to overlap.
325	
326	The instruction has the signature `[i32 i32 i32] -> []`. The parameters are, in order:
327	
328	- top-2: destination address
329	- top-1: source address
330	- top-0: size of memory region in bytes
331	
332	A trap occurs if:
333	
334	* the source offset plus size is greater than the length of the source memory   
335	* the destination offset plus size is greater than the length of the target memory   
336	
337	The bounds check is performed before any data are written.
338	
339	### `memory.fill` instruction
340	
341	Set all bytes in a memory region to a given byte. This instruction has an
342	immediate argument of which memory to operate on, and it must be zero for now.
343	
344	The instruction has the signature `[i32 i32 i32] -> []`. The parameters are, in order:
345	
346	- top-2: destination address
347	- top-1: byte value to set
348	- top-0: size of memory region in bytes
349	
350	A trap occurs if:
351	
352	* the destination offset plus size is greater than the length of the target memory
353	
354	The bounds check is performed before any data are written.
355	
356	
357	### `table.init`, `elem.drop`, and `table.copy` instructions
358	
359	The `table.*` instructions behave similarly to the `memory.*` instructions, with
360	the difference that they operate on element segments and tables, instead of
361	data segments and memories. The offset and length operands of `table.init` and
362	`table.copy` have element units instead of bytes as well.
363	
364	## Passive Segment Initialization Example
365	
366	Consider if there are two data sections, the first is always active and the
367	second is conditionally active if global 0 has a non-zero value. This could be
368	implemented as follows:
369	
370	```webassembly
371	(import "a" "global" (global i32))  ;; global 0
372	(memory 1)
373	(data (i32.const 0) "hello")   ;; data segment 0, is active so always copied
374	(data "goodbye")               ;; data segment 1, is passive
375	
376	(func $start
377	  (if (global.get 0)
378	
379	    ;; copy data segment 1 into memory 0 (the 0 is implicit)
380	    (memory.init 1
381	      (i32.const 16)    ;; target offset
382	      (i32.const 0)     ;; source offset
383	      (i32.const 7))    ;; length
384	
385	    ;; The memory used by this segment is no longer needed, so this segment can
386	    ;; be dropped.
387	    (data.drop 1))
388	)
389	(start $start)
390	```
391	
392	### Instruction encoding
393	
394	All bulk memory instructions are encoded as a 0xfc prefix byte, followed by
395	another opcode, optionally followed by more immediates:
396	
397	```
398	instr ::= ...
399	        | 0xfc operation:uint8 ...
400	```
401	
402	| Name | Opcode | Immediate | Description |
403	| ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
404	| `memory.init` | `0xfc 0x08` | `segment:varuint32`, `memory:0x00` | copy from a passive data segment to linear memory |
405	| `data.drop` | `0xfc 0x09` | `segment:varuint32` | prevent further use of passive data segment |
406	| `memory.copy` | `0xfc 0x0a` | `memory_dst:0x00` `memory_src:0x00` | copy from one region of linear memory to another region |
407	| `memory.fill` | `0xfc 0x0b` | `memory:0x00` | fill a region of linear memory with a given byte value |
408	| `table.init` | `0xfc 0x0c` | `segment:varuint32`, `table:0x00` | copy from a passive element segment to a table |
409	| `elem.drop` | `0xfc 0x0d` | `segment:varuint32` | prevent further use of a passive element segment |
410	| `table.copy` | `0xfc 0x0e` | `table_dst:0x00` `table_src:0x00` | copy from one region of a table to another region |
411	
412	### `DataCount` section
413	
414	The WebAssembly binary format is designed to be validated in a single pass. If
415	a section requires information to validate, it is guaranteed that this
416	information will be present in a previous section.
417	
418	The `memory.{init,drop}` instructions break this guarantee. Both of these
419	instructions are used in the `Code` section. They each have a data segment
420	index immediate, but the vector of data segments is not available until the
421	`Data` section is parsed, which occurs after the `Code` section.
422	
423	To keep single-pass validation, the number of data segments defined in the
424	`Data` section must be available before the `Code` section. This information is
425	provided in a new `DataCount` section with the code `12`.
426	
427	Like all sections, the `DataCount` section is optional. If present, it must
428	appear in the following order:
429	
430	| Section Name | Code | Description |
431	| ------------ | ---- | ----------- |
432	| Type | `1` | Function signature declarations |
433	| Import | `2` | Import declarations |
434	| Function | `3` | Function declarations |
435	| Table | `4` | Indirect function table and other tables |
436	| Memory | `5` | Memory attributes |
437	| Global | `6` | Global declarations |
438	| Export | `7` | Exports |
439	| Start | `8` | Start function declaration |
440	| Element | `9` | Elements section |
441	| DataCount | `12` | Data segment count |
442	| Code | `10` | Function bodies (code) |
443	| Data | `11` | Data segments |
444	
445	The `DataCount` section has just one field that specifies the number of data
446	segments in the `Data` section:
447	
448	| Field | Type | Description |
449	| ----- | ---- | ----------- |
450	| count | `varuint32` | count of data segments in `Data` section |
451	
452	The binary is malformed if `count` is not equal to the number of data segments
453	in the `Data` section. The binary is also malformed if the `DataCount` section
454	is omitted and a `memory.init` or `data.drop` instruction is used.
455

1	# Multi-value Extension
2	
3	## Introduction
4	
5	### Background
6	
7	* Currently, functions and instructions consume multiple operands but can produce at most one result
8	  - functions: `value* -> value?`
9	  - instructions: `value* -> value?`
10	  - blocks: `[] -> value?`
11	
12	* In a stack machine, these asymmetries are artificial restrictions
13	  - were imposed to simplify the initial WebAssembly release (multiple results deferred to post-MVP)
14	  - can easily be lifted by generalising to value* -> value*
15	
16	* Generalised semantics is well-understood
17	  - https://github.com/WebAssembly/spec/tree/main/papers/pldi2017.pdf
18	
19	* Semi-complete implementation of multiple results in V8
20	
21	
22	### Motivation
23	
24	* Multiple return values for functions:
25	  - enable unboxing of tuples or structs returned by value
26	  - efficient compilation of multiple return values
27	
28	* Multiple results for instructions:
29	  - enable instructions producing several results (divmod, arithmetics with carry)
30	
31	* Inputs to blocks:
32	  - loop labels can have arguments
33	  - can represent phis on backward edges
34	  - enable future `pick` operator to cross block boundary
35	  - macro definability of instructions with inputs
36	    * `i32.select3` = `dup if ... else ... end`
37	
38	
39	## Examples
40	
41	### Functions with multiple return Values
42	
43	A simple swap function.
44	```wasm
45	(func $swap (param i32 i32) (result i32 i32)
46		(local.get 1) (local.get 0)
47	)
48	```
49	
50	An addition function returning an additional carry bit.
51	```wasm
52	(func $add64_u_with_carry (param $i i64) (param $j i64) (param $c i32) (result i64 i32)
53		(local $k i64)
54		(local.set $k
55			(i64.add (i64.add (local.get $i) (local.get $j)) (i64.extend_i32_u (local.get $c)))
56		)
57		(return (local.get $k) (i64.lt_u (local.get $k) (local.get $i)))
58	)
59	```
60	
61	### Instructions with multiple results
62	
63	* `iNN.divrem` : \[iNN iNN\] -> \[iNN iNN\]
64	* `iNN.add_carry` : \[iNN iNN i32\] -> \[iNN i32\]
65	* `iNN.sub_carry` : \[iNN iNN i32\] -> \[iNN i32\]
66	* etc.
67	
68	
69	### Blocks with inputs
70	
71	Conditionally manipulating a stack operand without using a local.
72	```wasm
73	(func $add64_u_saturated (param i64 i64) (result i64)
74		(call $add64_u_with_carry (local.get 0) (local.get 1) (i32.const 0))
75		(if (param i64) (result i64)
76			(then (drop) (i64.const 0xffff_ffff_ffff_ffff))
77		)
78	)
79	```
80	
81	An iterative factorial function whose loop doesn't use locals, but uses arguments like phis.
82	```wasm
83	(func $pick0 (param i64) (result i64 i64)
84		(local.get 0) (local.get 0)
85	)
86	
87	(func $pick1 (param i64 i64) (result i64 i64 i64)
88		(local.get 0) (local.get 1) (local.get 0)
89	)
90	
91	(func $fac (param i64) (result i64)
92		(i64.const 1) (local.get 0)
93		(loop $l (param i64 i64) (result i64)
94			(call $pick1) (call $pick1) (i64.mul)
95			(call $pick1) (i64.const 1) (i64.sub)
96			(call $pick0) (i64.const 0) (i64.gt_u)
97			(br_if $l)
98			(call $pick1) (return)
99		)
100	)
101	```
102	
103	Macro definition of an instruction expanding into an `if`.
104	```
105	i64.select3  =
106	     dup if (param i64 i64 i64 i32) (result i64) … select ... else … end
107	```
108	
109	Macro expansion of `if` itself.
110	```
111	if (param t*) (result u*) A else B end  =
112	      block (param t* i32) (result u*)
113	          block (param t* i32) (result t*) (br_if 0)  B  (br 1) end  A
114	      end
115	```
116	
117	
118	## Spec Changes
119	
120	### Structure
121	
122	The structure of the language is mostly unaffected. The only changes are to the type syntax:
123	
124	* *resulttype* is generalised from \[*valtype*?\] to \[*valtype*\*\]
125	* block types (in `block`, `loop`, `if` instructions) are generalised from *resulttype* to *functype*
126	
127	
128	### Validation
129	
130	Arity restrictions are removed:
131	
132	* no arity check is imposed for valid *functype*
133	* all occurrences of superscript "?" are replaced with superscript "\*" (e.g. blocks, calls, return)
134	
135	Validation for block instructions is generalised:
136	
137	* The type of `block`, `loop`, and `if` is the *functype* \[t1\*\] -> \[t2\*\] given as the block type
138	* The type of the label of `block` and `if` is \[t2\*\]
139	* The type of the label of `loop` is \[t1\*\]
140	
141	
142	### Execution
143	
144	Nothing much needs to be done for multiple results:
145	
146	* replace all occurrences of superscript "?" with superscript "\*".
147	
148	The only non-mechanical change involves entering blocks with operands:
149	
150	* The operand values are popped of the stack, and pushed right back after the label.
151	* See paper for formulation of formal reduction rules
152	
153	
154	### Binary Format
155	
156	The binary requires a change to allow function types as block types. That requires extending the current ad-hoc encoding to allow references to function types.
157	
158	* `blocktype` is extended to the following format:
159	  ```
160	  blocktype ::= 0x40       => [] -> []
161	             |  t:valtype  => [] -> [t]
162	             |  ft:typeidx => ft
163	  ```
164	
165	### Text Format
166	
167	The text format is mostly unaffected, except that the syntax for block types is generalised:
168	
169	* `resulttype` is replaced with `blocktype`, whose syntax is
170	  ```
171	  blocktype ::= vec(param) vec(result)
172	  ```
173	
174	* `block`, `loop`, and `if` instructions contain a `blocktype` instead of `resulttype`.
175	
176	* The existing abbreviations for functions apply to block types.
177	
178	
179	### Soundness Proof
180	
181	The typing of administrative instructions need to be generalised, see the paper.
182	
183	
184	## Possible Alternatives and Extensions
185	
186	### More Flexible Block and Function Types
187	
188	* Instead of inline function types, could use references to the type section
189	  - more bureaucracy in the semantics, but otherwise no problem
190	
191	* Could also allow both
192	  - inline function types are slightly more compact for one-off uses
193	
194	* Could even unify the encoding of block types with function types everywhere
195	  - allow inline types even for functions, for the same benefits
196	
197	
198	## Open Questions
199	
200	* Destructuring or reshuffling multiple values requires locals, is that enough?
201	  - could add `pick` instruction (generalised `dup`)
202	  - could add `let` instruction (if you squint, a generalised `swap`)
203	  - different use cases?
204

1	# WebAssembly 128-bit packed SIMD Extension
2	
3	This specification describes a 128-bit packed *Single Instruction Multiple
4	Data* (SIMD) extension to WebAssembly that can be implemented efficiently on
5	current popular instruction set architectures.
6	
7	See also [The binary encoding of SIMD instructions](BinarySIMD.md).
8	
9	## Motivation
10	
11	WebAssembly aims to take advantage of [common hardware capabilities](https://github.com/WebAssembly/design/blob/master/Portability.md#assumptions-for-efficient-execution)
12	for near native speed. The motivation for this proposal is to introduce
13	WebAssembly operations that map to commonly available [SIMD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIMD)
14	instructions in hardware. 
15	
16	SIMD instructions in hardware work by performing simultaneous computations over
17	packed data in one instruction. These are commonly used to improve performance
18	for multimedia applications. The set of SIMD instructions in hardware is large, 
19	and varies across different versions of hardware. This proposal is comprised
20	of a portable subset of operations that in most cases map to commonly used
21	instructions in modern hardware. 
22	
23	
24	# Types
25	
26	WebAssembly is extended with a new `v128` value type and a number of new kinds
27	of immediate operands used by the SIMD instructions.
28	
29	## SIMD value type
30	
31	The `v128` value type is the _only_ type introduced in this extension. It has a
32	concrete mapping to a 128-bit representation with bits numbered 0–127. The
33	`v128` type corresponds to a vector register in a typical SIMD ISA. The
34	interpretation of the 128 bits in the vector register is provided by the
35	individual instructions. When a `v128` value is represented as 16 bytes, bits
36	0-7 go in the first byte with bit 0 as the LSB, bits 8-15 go in the second byte,
37	etc.
38	
39	## Immediate operands
40	
41	Some of the new SIMD instructions defined here have immediate operands that are
42	encoded as individual bytes in the binary encoding. Many have a limited valid
43	range, and it is a validation error if the immediate operands are out of range.
44	
45	* `ImmByte`: A single unconstrained byte (0-255).
46	* `ImmLaneIdx2`: A byte with values in the range 0–1 identifying a lane.
47	* `ImmLaneIdx4`: A byte with values in the range 0–3 identifying a lane.
48	* `ImmLaneIdx8`: A byte with values in the range 0–7 identifying a lane.
49	* `ImmLaneIdx16`: A byte with values in the range 0–15 identifying a lane.
50	* `ImmLaneIdx32`: A byte with values in the range 0–31 identifying a lane.
51	
52	## Operations on the SIMD value type
53	
54	The _single_ `v128` SIMD type can be used to represent different types of packed
55	data, e.g., it can represent four 32-bit floating point values, 8 16-bit signed
56	or unsigned integer values, etc.
57	
58	The instructions introduced in this specification are named according to the
59	following schema: `{interpretation}.{operation}`. Where the `{interpretation}`
60	prefix denotes how the bytes of the `v128` type are interpreted by the `{operation}`. 
61	
62	For example, the instructions `f32x4.extract_lane` and `i64x2.extract_lane`
63	perform the same semantic operation: extracting the scalar value of a vector
64	lane. However, the `f32x4.extract_lane` instruction returns a 32-bit wide
65	floating point value, while the `i64x2.extract_lane` instruction returns a
66	64-bit wide integer value.
67	
68	The `v128` vector type interpretation interprets the vector as a bag of bits. 
69	The `v{lane_width}x{n}` interpretations (e.g. `v32x4`) interpret the vector as
70	`n` lanes of `lane_width` bits. The `{t}{lane_width}x{n}` interpretations (e.g.
71	`i32x4` or `f32x4`) interpret the vector as `n` lanes of type `{t}{lane_width}`.
72	
73	### Lane division interpretation
74	
75	The first level of interpretations of the `v128` type imposes a lane structure on
76	the bits:
77	
78	* `v8x16 : v128`: 8-bit lanes numbered 0–15. Lane n corresponds to bits 8n – 8n+7.
79	* `v16x8 : v128`: 16-bit lanes numbered 0–7. Lane n corresponds to bits 16n – 16n+15.
80	* `v32x4 : v128`: 32-bit lanes numbered 0–3. Lane n corresponds to bits 32n – 32n+31.
81	* `v64x2 : v128`: 64-bit lanes numbered 0–1. Lane n corresponds to bits 64n – 64n+63.
82	
83	The lane dividing interpretations don't say anything about the semantics of the
84	bits in each lane. The interpretations have *properties* used by the semantic
85	specification pseudo-code below:
86	
87	|    S    | S.LaneBits | S.Lanes | S.MaskType |
88	|---------|-----------:|--------:|:----------:|
89	| `v8x16` |          8 |      16 | `i8x16`    |
90	| `v16x8` |         16 |       8 | `i16x8`    |
91	| `v32x4` |         32 |       4 | `i32x4`    |
92	| `v64x2` |         64 |       2 | `i64x2`    |
93	
94	Since WebAssembly is little-endian, the least significant bit in each lane is
95	the bit with the lowest number.
96	
97	### Modulo integer interpretations
98	
99	The bits in a lane can be interpreted as integers with modulo arithmetic
100	semantics. Many arithmetic operations can be defined on these types which don't
101	impose a signed or unsigned integer interpretation.
102	
103	* `i8x16 : v8x16`: Each lane is an `i8`.
104	* `i16x8 : v16x8`: Each lane is an `i16`.
105	* `i32x4 : v32x4`: Each lane is an `i32`.
106	* `i64x2 : v64x2`: Each lane is an `i64`.
107	
108	Additional properties:
109	
110	|    S    |  S.Smin | S.Smax | S.Umax |
111	|---------|--------:|-------:|-------:|
112	| `i8x16` |    -2^7 |  2^7-1 |  2^8-1 |
113	| `i16x8` |   -2^15 | 2^15-1 | 2^16-1 |
114	| `i32x4` |   -2^31 | 2^31-1 | 2^32-1 |
115	| `i64x2` |   -2^63 | 2^63-1 | 2^64-1 |
116	
117	Some operations interpret each lane specifically as a signed or unsigned
118	integer. These operations have `_s` and `_u` suffixes as is the convention is
119	WebAssembly.
120	
121	### Floating-point interpretations
122	
123	Each lane is interpreted as an IEEE floating-point number.
124	
125	* `f32x4 : v32x4`: Each lane is an `f32`.
126	* `f64x2 : v64x2`: Each lane is an `f64`.
127	
128	The floating-point operations in this specification aim to be compatible with
129	WebAssembly's scalar floating-point operations. In particular, the rules about
130	NaN propagation and default NaN values are the same, and all operations use the
131	default *roundTiesToEven* rounding mode.
132	
133	# JavaScript API and SIMD Values
134	
135	Accessing WebAssembly module imports or exports containing SIMD Type from JavaScript will throw.
136	
137	### Module Function Imports
138	
139	Calling an imported function from JavaScript when the function arguments or result is of type v128 will cause the host function to immediately throw a [`TypeError`](https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-native-error-types-used-in-this-standard-typeerror).
140	
141	### Exported Function Exotic Objects
142	
143	Invoking the [[Call]] method of an Exported Function Exotic Object when the function type of its [[Closure]] has an argument or result of type v128 will cause the host function to immediately throw a [`TypeError`](https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-native-error-types-used-in-this-standard-typeerror).
144	
145	
146	## WebAssembly Module Instantiation
147	
148	Instantiating a WebAssembly Module from a Module moduleObject will throw a LinkError exception, when the global's valtype is v128 and the imported objects type is not WebAssembly.Global. 
149	
150	## Exported Functions
151	
152	### Exported Function Call
153	
154	Calling an Exported Function will throw a [`TypeError`](https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-native-error-types-used-in-this-standard-typeerror), when parameters or results contains a v128. This error is thrown each time the [[Call]] method is invoked.
155	
156	### Creating a host function
157	
158	Creating a host function from JavaScript object will throw a [`TypeError`](https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-native-error-types-used-in-this-standard-typeerror), when the host function signature contains a v128.
159	
160	### Global constructor
161	
162	If Global(descriptor, v) constructor will throw a [`TypeError`](https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-native-error-types-used-in-this-standard-typeerror), when invoked with v of valuetype v128.
163	
164	## JavaScript coercion
165	
166	### ToJSValue
167	
168	The algorithm toJSValue(w) should have an assertion ensuring w is not of the form v128.const v128.
169	
170	### ToWebAssemblyValue
171	
172	The algorithm ToWebAssemblyValue(v, type)  should have an assertion ensuring type is not v128.
173	
174	## JavaScript API Global Object algorithms
175	
176	### ToValueType
177	
178	The algorithm ToValueType(s) will return 'v128' if s equals "v128".
179	
180	### DefaultValue 
181	
182	The algorithm DefaultValueType(valueType) will return v128.const 0.
183	
184	### GetGlobalValue
185	
186	The algorithm GetGlobalValue(Global global) will throw a [`TypeError`](https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-native-error-types-used-in-this-standard-typeerror), when type_global(store, global.[[Global]]) is of the form mut v128.
187	
188	### Global value attribute Setter
189	
190	The setter of the value attribute of Global will throw a [`TypeError`](https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-native-error-types-used-in-this-standard-typeerror), when invoked with a value v of valuetype v128.
191	
192	# Operations
193	
194	The SIMD operations described in this sections are generally named
195	`S.Op`, where `S` is either a SIMD type or one of the interpretations
196	of a SIMD type. Immediate mode operands are prefixed with `imm`.
197	
198	Many operations are simply the lane-wise application of a scalar operation:
199	
200	```python
201	def S.lanewise_unary(func, a):
202	    result = S.New()
203	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
204	        result[i] = func(a[i])
205	    return result
206	
207	def S.lanewise_binary(func, a, b):
208	    result = S.New()
209	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
210	        result[i] = func(a[i], b[i])
211	    return result
212	```
213	
214	Comparison operators produce a mask vector where the bits in each lane are 0
215	for false and all ones for true:
216	
217	```python
218	def S.lanewise_comparison(func, a, b):
219	    all_ones = S.MaskType.Umax
220	    result = S.MaskType.New()
221	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
222	        result[i] = all_ones if func(a[i], b[i]) else 0
223	    return result
224	```
225	
226	## Constructing SIMD values
227	
228	### Constant
229	* `v128.const(imm: ImmByte[16]) -> v128`
230	
231	Materialize a constant `v128` SIMD value from the 16 immediate bytes in the
232	immediate mode operand `imm` . The `v128.const` instruction is encoded with 16
233	immediate bytes which provide the bits of the vector directly.
234	
235	### Create vector with identical lanes
236	* `i8x16.splat(x: i32) -> v128`
237	* `i16x8.splat(x: i32) -> v128`
238	* `i32x4.splat(x: i32) -> v128`
239	* `i64x2.splat(x: i64) -> v128`
240	* `f32x4.splat(x: f32) -> v128`
241	* `f64x2.splat(x: f64) -> v128`
242	
243	Construct a vector with `x` replicated to all lanes:
244	
245	```python
246	def S.splat(x):
247	    result = S.New()
248	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
249	        result[i] = S.Reduce(x)
250	    return result
251	```
252	
253	## Accessing lanes
254	
255	### Extract lane as a scalar
256	* `i8x16.extract_lane_s(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx16) -> i32`
257	* `i8x16.extract_lane_u(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx16) -> i32`
258	* `i16x8.extract_lane_s(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx8) -> i32`
259	* `i16x8.extract_lane_u(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx8) -> i32`
260	* `i32x4.extract_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx4) -> i32`
261	* `i64x2.extract_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx2) -> i64`
262	* `f32x4.extract_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx4) -> f32`
263	* `f64x2.extract_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx2) -> f64`
264	
265	Extract the scalar value of lane specified in the immediate mode operand `imm`
266	in `a`. The `{interpretation}.extract_lane{_s}{_u}` instructions are encoded
267	with one immediate byte providing the index of the lane to extract.
268	
269	```python
270	def S.extract_lane(a, i):
271	    return a[i]
272	```
273	
274	The `_s` and `_u` variants will sign-extend or zero-extend the lane value to
275	`i32` respectively.
276	
277	### Replace lane value
278	* `i8x16.replace_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx16, x: i32) -> v128`
279	* `i16x8.replace_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx8, x: i32) -> v128`
280	* `i32x4.replace_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx4, x: i32) -> v128`
281	* `i64x2.replace_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx2, x: i64) -> v128`
282	* `f32x4.replace_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx4, x: f32) -> v128`
283	* `f64x2.replace_lane(a: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx2, x: f64) -> v128`
284	
285	Return a new vector with lanes identical to `a`, except for the lane specified
286	in the immediate mode operand `imm` which has the value `x`. The
287	`{interpretation}.replace_lane` instructions are encoded with an immediate byte 
288	providing the index of the lane the value of which is to be replaced.
289	
290	```python
291	def S.replace_lane(a, i, x):
292	    result = S.New()
293	    for j in range(S.Lanes):
294	        result[j] = a[j]
295	    result[i] = x
296	    return result
297	```
298	
299	The input lane value, `x`, is interpreted the same way as for the splat
300	instructions. For the `i8` and `i16` lanes, the high bits of `x` are ignored.
301	
302	### Shuffling using immediate indices
303	* `i8x16.shuffle(a: v128, b: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx32[16]) -> v128`
304	
305	Returns a new vector with lanes selected from the lanes of the two input vectors
306	`a` and `b` specified in the 16 byte wide immediate mode operand `imm`. This
307	instruction is encoded with 16 bytes providing the indices of the elements to
308	return. The indices `i` in range `[0, 15]` select the `i`-th element of `a`. The
309	indices in range `[16, 31]` select the `i - 16`-th element of `b`.
310	
311	```python
312	def S.shuffle(a, b, s):
313	    result = S.New()
314	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
315	        if s[i] < S.lanes:
316	            result[i] = a[s[i]]
317	        else:
318	            result[i] = b[s[i] - S.lanes]
319	    return result
320	```
321	
322	### Swizzling using variable indices
323	* `i8x16.swizzle(a: v128, s: v128) -> v128`
324	
325	Returns a new vector with lanes selected from the lanes of the first input
326	vector `a` specified in the second input vector `s`. The indices `i` in range
327	`[0, 15]` select the `i`-th element of `a`. For indices outside of the range
328	the resulting lane is initialized to 0.
329	
330	```python
331	def S.swizzle(a, s):
332	    result = S.New()
333	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
334	        if s[i] < S.lanes:
335	            result[i] = a[s[i]]
336	        else:
337	            result[i] = 0
338	    return result
339	```

341	## Integer arithmetic
342	
343	Wrapping integer arithmetic discards the high bits of the result.
344	
345	```python
346	def S.Reduce(x):
347	    bitmask = (1 << S.LaneBits) - 1
348	    return x & bitmask
349	```
350	
351	There is no integer division operation provided here. This operation is not
352	commonly part of 128-bit SIMD ISAs.
353	
354	### Integer addition
355	* `i8x16.add(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
356	* `i16x8.add(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
357	* `i32x4.add(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
358	* `i64x2.add(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
359	
360	Lane-wise wrapping integer addition:
361	
362	```python
363	def S.add(a, b):
364	    def add(x, y):
365	        return S.Reduce(x + y)
366	    return S.lanewise_binary(add, a, b)
367	```
368	
369	### Integer subtraction
370	* `i8x16.sub(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
371	* `i16x8.sub(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
372	* `i32x4.sub(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
373	* `i64x2.sub(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
374	
375	Lane-wise wrapping integer subtraction:
376	
377	```python
378	def S.sub(a, b):
379	    def sub(x, y):
380	        return S.Reduce(x - y)
381	    return S.lanewise_binary(sub, a, b)
382	```
383	
384	### Integer multiplication
385	* `i16x8.mul(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
386	* `i32x4.mul(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
387	* `i64x2.mul(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
388	
389	Lane-wise wrapping integer multiplication:
390	
391	```python
392	def S.mul(a, b):
393	    def mul(x, y):
394	        return S.Reduce(x * y)
395	    return S.lanewise_binary(mul, a, b)
396	```
397	
398	### Integer dot product
399	* `i32x4.dot_i16x8_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
400	
401	Lane-wise multiply signed 16-bit integers in the two input vectors and add adjacent pairs of the full 32-bit results.
402	
403	### Integer negation
404	* `i8x16.neg(a: v128) -> v128`
405	* `i16x8.neg(a: v128) -> v128`
406	* `i32x4.neg(a: v128) -> v128`
407	* `i64x2.neg(a: v128) -> v128`
408	
409	Lane-wise wrapping integer negation. In wrapping arithmetic, `y = -x` is the
410	unique value such that `x + y == 0`.
411	
412	```python
413	def S.neg(a):
414	    def neg(x):
415	        return S.Reduce(-x)
416	    return S.lanewise_unary(neg, a)
417	```
418	
419	## Extended integer arithmetic
420	
421	### Extended integer multiplication
422	* `i16x8.extmul_low_i8x16_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
423	* `i16x8.extmul_high_i8x16_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
424	* `i16x8.extmul_low_i8x16_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
425	* `i16x8.extmul_high_i8x16_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
426	* `i32x4.extmul_low_i16x8_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
427	* `i32x4.extmul_high_i16x8_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
428	* `i32x4.extmul_low_i16x8_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`

457	Lane-wise integer extended pairwise addition producing extended results (twice wider results than the inputs).
458	
459	```python

461	    result = S.New()
462	    for i in range(S.Lanes):

472	## Saturating integer arithmetic
473	
474	Saturating integer arithmetic behaves differently on signed and unsigned lanes.
475	It is only defined here for 8-bit and 16-bit integer lanes.
476	
477	```python
478	def S.SignedSaturate(x):
479	    if x < S.Smin:
480	        return S.Smin
481	    if x > S.Smax:
482	        return S.Smax
483	    return x
484	
485	def S.UnsignedSaturate(x):
486	    if x < 0:
487	        return 0
488	    if x > S.Umax:
489	        return S.Umax
490	    return x
491	```
492	
493	### Saturating integer addition
494	* `i8x16.add_sat_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
495	* `i8x16.add_sat_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
496	* `i16x8.add_sat_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
497	* `i16x8.add_sat_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
498	
499	Lane-wise saturating addition:
500	
501	```python
502	def S.add_sat_s(a, b):
503	    def addsat(x, y):
504	        return S.SignedSaturate(x + y)
505	    return S.lanewise_binary(addsat, S.AsSigned(a), S.AsSigned(b))
506	
507	def S.add_sat_u(a, b):
508	    def addsat(x, y):
509	        return S.UnsignedSaturate(x + y)
510	    return S.lanewise_binary(addsat, S.AsUnsigned(a), S.AsUnsigned(b))
511	```
512	
513	### Saturating integer subtraction
514	* `i8x16.sub_sat_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
515	* `i8x16.sub_sat_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
516	* `i16x8.sub_sat_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
517	* `i16x8.sub_sat_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
518	
519	Lane-wise saturating subtraction:
520	
521	```python
522	def S.sub_sat_s(a, b):
523	    def subsat(x, y):
524	        return S.SignedSaturate(x - y)
525	    return S.lanewise_binary(subsat, S.AsSigned(a), S.AsSigned(b))
526	
527	def S.sub_sat_u(a, b):
528	    def subsat(x, y):
529	        return S.UnsignedSaturate(x - y)
530	    return S.lanewise_binary(subsat, S.AsUnsigned(a), S.AsUnsigned(b))
531	```

533	### Saturating integer Q-format rounding multiplication
534	
535	* `i16x8.q15mulr_sat_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`

537	Lane-wise saturating rounding multiplication in Q15 format:
538	
539	```python

542	        return S.SignedSaturate((x * y + 0x4000) >> 15)
543	    return S.lanewise_binary(subq15mulr, S.AsSigned(a), S.AsSigned(b))

605	## Bit shifts
606	
607	### Left shift by scalar
608	* `i8x16.shl(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
609	* `i16x8.shl(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
610	* `i32x4.shl(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
611	* `i64x2.shl(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
612	
613	Shift the bits in each lane to the left by the same amount. The shift count is
614	taken modulo lane width:
615	
616	```python
617	def S.shl(a, y):
618	    # Number of bits to shift: 0 .. S.LaneBits - 1.
619	    amount = y mod S.LaneBits
620	    def shift(x):
621	        return S.Reduce(x << amount)
622	    return S.lanewise_unary(shift, a)
623	```
624	
625	### Right shift by scalar
626	* `i8x16.shr_s(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
627	* `i8x16.shr_u(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
628	* `i16x8.shr_s(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
629	* `i16x8.shr_u(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
630	* `i32x4.shr_s(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
631	* `i32x4.shr_u(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
632	* `i64x2.shr_s(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
633	* `i64x2.shr_u(a: v128, y: i32) -> v128`
634	
635	Shift the bits in each lane to the right by the same amount. The shift count is
636	taken modulo lane width.  This is an arithmetic right shift for the `_s`
637	variants and a logical right shift for the `_u` variants.
638	
639	```python
640	def S.shr_s(a, y):
641	    # Number of bits to shift: 0 .. S.LaneBits - 1.
642	    amount = y mod S.LaneBits
643	    def shift(x):
644	        return x >> amount
645	    return S.lanewise_unary(shift, S.AsSigned(a))
646	
647	def S.shr_u(a, y):
648	    # Number of bits to shift: 0 .. S.LaneBits - 1.
649	    amount = y mod S.LaneBits
650	    def shift(x):
651	        return x >> amount
652	    return S.lanewise_unary(shift, S.AsUnsigned(a))
653	```

656	## Bitwise operations
657	
658	Bitwise operations treat a `v128` value type as a vector of 128 independent bits.
659	
660	### Bitwise logic
661	* `v128.and(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
662	* `v128.or(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
663	* `v128.xor(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
664	* `v128.not(a: v128) -> v128`
665	
666	The logical operations defined on the scalar integer types are also available
667	on the `v128` type where they operate bitwise the same way C's `&`, `|`, `^`,
668	and `~` operators work on an `unsigned` type.
669	
670	### Bitwise AND-NOT
671	
672	* `v128.andnot(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
673	
674	Bitwise AND of bits of `a` and the logical inverse of bits of `b`. This operation is equivalent to `v128.and(a, v128.not(b))`.
675	
676	### Bitwise select
677	* `v128.bitselect(v1: v128, v2: v128, c: v128) -> v128`
678	
679	Use the bits in the control mask `c` to select the corresponding bit from `v1`
680	when 1 and `v2` when 0.
681	This is the same as `v128.or(v128.and(v1, c), v128.and(v2, v128.not(c)))`.
682	
683	Note that the normal WebAssembly `select` instruction also works with vector
684	types. It selects between two whole vectors controlled by a single scalar value,
685	rather than selecting bits controlled by a control mask vector.
686	
687	### Lane-wise Population Count
688	* `i8x16.popcnt(v: v128) -> v128`
689	
690	Count the number of bits set to one within each lane.
691	
692	```python
693	def S.popcnt(v):
694	    return S.lanewise_unary(popcnt, v)
695	```
696	
697	## Boolean horizontal reductions
698	
699	These operations reduce all the lanes of an integer vector to a single scalar
700	0 or 1 value. A lane is considered "true" if it is non-zero.
701	
702	### Any bit true
703	* `v128.any_true(a: v128) -> i32`
704	
705	These functions return 1 if any bit in `a` is non-zero, 0 otherwise.
706	
707	### All lanes true
708	* `i8x16.all_true(a: v128) -> i32`
709	* `i16x8.all_true(a: v128) -> i32`
710	* `i32x4.all_true(a: v128) -> i32`
711	* `i64x2.all_true(a: v128) -> i32`
712	
713	These functions return 1 if all lanes in `a` are non-zero, 0 otherwise.
714	
715	```python
716	def S.all_true(a):
717	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
718	        if a[i] == 0:
719	            return 0
720	    return 1
721	```

723	## Bitmask extraction
724	
725	* `i8x16.bitmask(a: v128) -> i32`
726	* `i16x8.bitmask(a: v128) -> i32`
727	* `i32x4.bitmask(a: v128) -> i32`
728	* `i64x2.bitmask(a: v128) -> i32`
729	
730	These operations extract the high bit for each lane in `a` and produce a scalar
731	mask with all bits concatenated.
732	
733	```python
734	def S.bitmask(a):
735	    result = 0
736	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
737	        if a[i] < 0:
738	            result = result | (1 << i)
739	    return result
740	```

742	## Comparisons
743	
744	The comparison operations all compare two vectors lane-wise, and produce a mask
745	vector with the same number of lanes as the input interpretation where the bits
746	in each lane are `0` for `false` and all ones for `true`.
747	
748	### Equality
749	* `i8x16.eq(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
750	* `i16x8.eq(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
751	* `i32x4.eq(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
752	* `i64x2.eq(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
753	* `f32x4.eq(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
754	* `f64x2.eq(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
755	
756	Integer equality is independent of the signed/unsigned interpretation. Floating
757	point equality follows IEEE semantics, so a NaN lane compares not equal with
758	anything, including itself, and +0.0 is equal to -0.0:
759	
760	```python
761	def S.eq(a, b):
762	    def eq(x, y):
763	        return x == y
764	    return S.lanewise_comparison(eq, a, b)
765	```
766	
767	### Non-equality
768	* `i8x16.ne(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`

782	```

828	## Load and store
829	
830	Load and store operations are provided for the `v128` vectors. The memory
831	operations take the same arguments and have the same semantics as the existing
832	scalar WebAssembly load and store instructions (see
833	[memarg](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/bikeshed/index.html#syntax-memarg).
834	The difference is that the memory access size is 16 bytes which is also the
835	natural alignment.
836	
837	### Load
838	
839	* `v128.load(m: memarg) -> v128`
840	
841	Load a `v128` vector from the given heap address.
842	
843	```python
844	def S.load(m: memarg):
845	    return S.from_bytes(memory[memarg.offset:memarg.offset + 16])
846	```
847	
848	### Load and Zero-Pad
849	
850	* `v128.load32_zero(m: memarg) -> v128`
851	* `v128.load64_zero(m: memarg) -> v128`
852	
853	Load a single 32-bit or 64-bit element into the lowest bits of a `v128` vector,
854	and initialize all other bits of the `v128` vector to zero.
855	
856	```python
857	def S.load32_zero(m: memarg):
858	    return S.from_bytes(memory[memarg.offset:memarg.offset + 4])
859	```
860	
861	```python
862	def S.load64_zero(m: memarg):
863	    return S.from_bytes(memory[memarg.offset:memarg.offset + 8])
864	```
865	
866	### Load and Splat
867	
868	* `v128.load8_splat(m: memarg) -> v128`
869	* `v128.load16_splat(m: memarg) -> v128`
870	* `v128.load32_splat(m: memarg) -> v128`
871	* `v128.load64_splat(m: memarg) -> v128`
872	
873	Load a single element and splat to all lanes of a `v128` vector. The natural
874	alignment is the size of the element loaded.
875	
876	```python
877	def S.load_splat(m: memarg):
878	    val_bytes = memory[memarg.offset:memarg.offset + S.LaneBytes])
879	    return S.splat(S.LaneType.from_bytes(val_bytes))
880	```
881	
882	### Load Lane
883	
884	* `v128.load8_lane(m: memarg, x: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx16) -> v128`
885	* `v128.load16_lane(m: memarg, x: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx8) -> v128`
886	* `v128.load32_lane(m: memarg, x: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx4) -> v128`
887	* `v128.load64_lane(m: memarg, x: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx2) -> v128`
888	
889	Load a single element from `m` into the lane of `x` specified in the immediate
890	mode operand `imm`. The values of all other lanes of `x` are bypassed as is.
891	
892	### Load and Extend
893	
894	* `v128.load8x8_s(m: memarg) -> v128`: load eight 8-bit integers and sign extend each one to a 16-bit lane
895	* `v128.load8x8_u(m: memarg) -> v128`: load eight 8-bit integers and zero extend each one to a 16-bit lane
896	* `v128.load16x4_s(m: memarg) -> v128`: load four 16-bit integers and sign extend each one to a 32-bit lane
897	* `v128.load16x4_u(m: memarg) -> v128`: load four 16-bit integers and zero extend each one to a 32-bit lane
898	* `v128.load32x2_s(m: memarg) -> v128`: load two 32-bit integers and sign extend each one to a 64-bit lane
899	* `v128.load32x2_u(m: memarg) -> v128`: load two 32-bit integers and zero extend each one to a 64-bit lane
900	
901	Fetch consecutive integers up to 32-bit wide and produce a vector with lanes up
902	to 64 bits. The natural alignment is 8 bytes.
903	
904	```python
905	def S.load_extend(ext, m: memarg):
906	    result = S.New()
907	    bytes = memory[memarg.offset:memarg.offset + 8])
908	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
909	        result[i] = ext(S.LaneType.from_bytes(bytes[(i * S.LaneBytes/2):((i+1) * S.LaneBytes/2)]))
910	    return result
911	
912	def S.load_extend_s(m: memarg):
913	    return S.load_extend(Sext, memarg)
914	
915	def S.load_extend_u(m: memarg):
916	    return S.load_extend(Zext, memarg)
917	```

919	### Store
920	
921	* `v128.store(m: memarg, data: v128)`
922	
923	Store a `v128` vector to the given heap address.
924	
925	```python
926	def S.store(m: memarg, a):
927	    memory[memarg.offset:memarg.offset + 16] = bytes(a)
928	```

930	### Store Lane
931	
932	* `v128.store8_lane(m: memarg, data: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx16)`
933	* `v128.store16_lane(m: memarg, data: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx8)`
934	* `v128.store32_lane(m: memarg, data: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx4)`
935	* `v128.store64_lane(m: memarg, data: v128, imm: ImmLaneIdx2)`
936	
937	Store into `m` the lane of `data` specified in the immediate mode operand `imm`.

939	## Floating-point sign bit operations
940	
941	These floating point operations are simple manipulations of the sign bit. No
942	changes are made to the exponent or trailing significand bits, even for NaN
943	inputs.
944	
945	### Negation
946	* `f32x4.neg(a: v128) -> v128`
947	* `f64x2.neg(a: v128) -> v128`
948	
949	Apply the IEEE `negate(x)` function to each lane. This simply inverts the sign
950	bit, preserving all other bits.
951	
952	```python
953	def S.neg(a):
954	    return S.lanewise_unary(ieee.negate, a)
955	```
956	
957	### Floating-point absolute value
958	* `f32x4.abs(a: v128) -> v128`
959	* `f64x2.abs(a: v128) -> v128`
960	
961	Apply the IEEE `abs(x)` function to each lane. This simply clears the sign bit,
962	preserving all other bits.
963	
964	```python
965	def S.abs(a):
966	    return S.lanewise_unary(ieee.abs, a)
967	```
968	
969	## Floating-point min and max
970	
971	These operations are not part of the IEEE 754-2008 standard. They are lane-wise
972	versions of the existing scalar WebAssembly operations.
973	
974	### NaN-propagating minimum
975	* `f32x4.min(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
976	* `f64x2.min(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
977	
978	Lane-wise minimum value, propagating NaNs.
979	
980	### NaN-propagating maximum
981	* `f32x4.max(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
982	* `f64x2.max(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
983	
984	Lane-wise maximum value, propagating NaNs.
985	
986	### Pseudo-minimum
987	* `f32x4.pmin(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
988	* `f64x2.pmin(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
989	
990	Lane-wise minimum value, defined as `b < a ? b : a`.
991	
992	### Pseudo-maximum
993	* `f32x4.pmax(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
994	* `f64x2.pmax(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
995	
996	Lane-wise maximum value, defined as `a < b ? b : a`.
997	
998	## Floating-point arithmetic
999	
1000	The floating-point arithmetic operations are all lane-wise versions of the
1001	existing scalar WebAssembly operations.
1002	
1003	### Addition
1004	* `f32x4.add(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1005	* `f64x2.add(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1006	
1007	Lane-wise IEEE `addition`.
1008	
1009	### Subtraction
1010	* `f32x4.sub(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1011	* `f64x2.sub(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1012	
1013	Lane-wise IEEE `subtraction`.
1014	
1015	### Division
1016	* `f32x4.div(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1017	* `f64x2.div(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1018	
1019	Lane-wise IEEE `division`.
1020	
1021	### Multiplication
1022	* `f32x4.mul(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1023	* `f64x2.mul(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1024	
1025	Lane-wise IEEE `multiplication`.
1026	
1027	### Square root
1028	* `f32x4.sqrt(a: v128) -> v128`
1029	* `f64x2.sqrt(a: v128) -> v128`
1030	
1031	Lane-wise IEEE `squareRoot`.
1032	
1033	### Round to integer above (ceiling)
1034	* `f32x4.ceil(a: v128) -> v128`
1035	* `f64x2.ceil(a: v128) -> v128`
1036	
1037	Lane-wise rounding to the nearest integral value not smaller than the input.
1038	
1039	### Round to integer below (floor)
1040	* `f32x4.floor(a: v128) -> v128`
1041	* `f64x2.floor(a: v128) -> v128`
1042	
1043	Lane-wise rounding to the nearest integral value not greater than the input.
1044	
1045	### Round to integer toward zero (truncate to integer)
1046	* `f32x4.trunc(a: v128) -> v128`
1047	* `f64x2.trunc(a: v128) -> v128`
1048	
1049	Lane-wise rounding to the nearest integral value with the magnitude not larger than the input.
1050	
1051	### Round to nearest integer, ties to even
1052	* `f32x4.nearest(a: v128) -> v128`
1053	* `f64x2.nearest(a: v128) -> v128`
1054	
1055	Lane-wise rounding to the nearest integral value; if two values are equally near, rounds to the even one.
1056	
1057	## Conversions
1058	### Integer to single-precision floating point
1059	* `f32x4.convert_i32x4_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1060	* `f32x4.convert_i32x4_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1061	
1062	Lane-wise conversion from integer to floating point. Integer values not
1063	representable as single-precision floating-point numbers will be rounded to the
1064	nearest-even representable number.
1065	
1066	### Integer to double-precision floating point
1067	* `f64x2.convert_low_i32x4_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1068	* `f64x2.convert_low_i32x4_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1069	
1070	Lane-wise conversion from integer to floating point.
1071	
1072	### Single-precision floating point to integer with saturation
1073	* `i32x4.trunc_sat_f32x4_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1074	* `i32x4.trunc_sat_f32x4_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1075	
1076	Lane-wise saturating conversion from single-precision floating point to integer
1077	using the IEEE `convertToIntegerTowardZero` function. If any input lane is a
1078	NaN, the resulting lane is 0. If the rounded integer value of a lane is outside
1079	the range of the destination type, the result is saturated to the nearest
1080	representable integer value.
1081	
1082	### Double-precision floating point to integer with saturation
1083	* `i32x4.trunc_sat_f64x2_s_zero(a: v128) -> v128`
1084	* `i32x4.trunc_sat_f64x2_u_zero(a: v128) -> v128`
1085	
1086	Saturating conversion of the two double-precision floating point lanes to two
1087	lower integer lanes using the IEEE `convertToIntegerTowardZero` function. The
1088	two higher lanes of the result are initialized to zero. If any input lane is a
1089	NaN, the resulting lane is 0. If the rounded integer value of a lane is outside
1090	the range of the destination type, the result is saturated to the nearest
1091	representable integer value.
1092	
1093	### Double-precision floating point to single-precision
1094	* `f32x4.demote_f64x2_zero(a: v128) -> v128`
1095	
1096	Conversion of the two double-precision floating point lanes to two lower
1097	single-precision lanes of the result. The two higher lanes of the result are
1098	initialized to zero. If the conversion result is not representable as a
1099	single-precision floating point number, it is rounded to the nearest-even
1100	representable number.
1101	
1102	### Single-precision floating point to double-precision
1103	* `f64x2.promote_low_f32x4(a: v128) -> v128`
1104	
1105	Conversion of the two lower single-precision floating point lanes to the two
1106	double-precision lanes of the result.
1107	
1108	### Integer to integer narrowing
1109	* `i8x16.narrow_i16x8_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1110	* `i8x16.narrow_i16x8_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1111	* `i16x8.narrow_i32x4_s(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1112	* `i16x8.narrow_i32x4_u(a: v128, b: v128) -> v128`
1113	
1114	Converts two input vectors into a smaller lane vector by narrowing each lane,
1115	signed or unsigned. The signed narrowing operation will use signed saturation
1116	to handle overflow, 0x7f or 0x80 for i8x16, the unsigned narrowing operation
1117	will use unsigned saturation to handle overflow, 0x00 or 0xff for i8x16.
1118	Regardless of the whether the operation is signed or unsigned, the input lanes
1119	are interpreted as signed integers.
1120	
1121	```python
1122	def S.narrow_T_s(a, b):
1123	    result = S.New()
1124	    for i in range(T.Lanes):
1125	        result[i] = S.SignedSaturate(a[i])
1126	    for i in range(T.Lanes):
1127	        result[T.Lanes + i] = S.SignedSaturate(b[i])
1128	    return result
1129	
1130	def S.narrow_T_u(a, b):
1131	    result = S.New()
1132	    for i in range(T.Lanes):
1133	        result[i] = S.UnsignedSaturate(a[i])
1134	    for i in range(T.Lanes):
1135	        result[T.Lanes + i] = S.UnsignedSaturate(b[i])
1136	    return result
1137	```
1138	
1139	### Integer to integer extension
1140	* `i16x8.extend_low_i8x16_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1141	* `i16x8.extend_high_i8x16_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1142	* `i16x8.extend_low_i8x16_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1143	* `i16x8.extend_high_i8x16_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1144	* `i32x4.extend_low_i16x8_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1145	* `i32x4.extend_high_i16x8_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1146	* `i32x4.extend_low_i16x8_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1147	* `i32x4.extend_high_i16x8_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1148	* `i64x2.extend_low_i32x4_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1149	* `i64x2.extend_high_i32x4_s(a: v128) -> v128`
1150	* `i64x2.extend_low_i32x4_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1151	* `i64x2.extend_high_i32x4_u(a: v128) -> v128`
1152	
1153	Converts low or high half of the smaller lane vector to a larger lane vector,
1154	sign extended or zero (unsigned) extended.
1155	
1156	```python
1157	def S.extend_low_T(ext, a):
1158	    result = S.New()
1159	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
1160	        result[i] = ext(a[i])
1161	
1162	def S.extend_high_T(ext, a):
1163	    result = S.New()
1164	    for i in range(S.Lanes):
1165	        result[i] = ext(a[S.Lanes + i])
1166	
1167	def S.extend_low_T_s(a):
1168	    return S.extend_low_T(Sext, a)
1169	
1170	def S.extend_high_T_s(a):
1171	    return S.extend_high_T(Sext, a)
1172	
1173	def S.extend_low_T_u(a):
1174	    return S.extend_low_T(Zext, a)
1175	
1176	def S.extend_high_T_u(a):
1177	    return S.extend_high_T(Zext, a)
1178	```

1	# Generated-code ABI
2	
3	The emitted `.ll` is compiled by the grader with LLVM 23 exactly like this,
4	**at both `-O0` and `-O2`**:
5	
6	```
7	clang -O0|-O2 -shared -fPIC -Wl,-Bsymbolic -o module.so OUTPUT.ll -lm
8	```
9	
10	The result is loaded with `dlopen` into a harness process, which drives it
11	through the ABI below. The harness is not part of this workspace; this file is
12	the complete contract.
13	
14	## Output requirements
15	
16	* The IR must be valid LLVM 23 IR and target `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`. You may
17	  omit the target triple or data layout, or set them to the usual x86-64 Linux values.
18	* The IR must have well-defined behavior for **every** input the original wasm
19	  module can receive. It must not rely on LLVM undefined behavior, `poison`, or
20	  `undef` for observable results. The code is compiled with optimizations, so
21	  any UB will be exploited.
22	* Floating point must follow WebAssembly semantics exactly. In particular, do not
23	  use fast-math flags (`fast`, `contract`, `nnan`, `nsz`, ...) that change results.
24	  `fma` contraction is not allowed. NaN payloads follow the wasm rules, and the
25	  tests accept any NaN wherever wasm allows any NaN.
26	* Each `.so` is one module instance. Use whatever global state you like, but give
27	  everything except the ABI symbols `internal`/`private` linkage.
28	* You may call functions from the C library and libm (for example `malloc`, `calloc`,
29	  `realloc`, `free`, `mmap`, `munmap`, `mremap`, `memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset`,
30	  `abort`, `ceilf`, ...) and any LLVM intrinsic.
31	* Do **not** install signal handlers or depend on hardware faults (guard pages,
32	  `SIGFPE`, ...) for wasm semantics. The harness owns signal handling. Bounds and
33	  trap conditions must be checked explicitly in the generated code. The one exception
34	  is native stack overflow, described below.
35	
36	## Slots and names
37	
38	All values cross the ABI in **16-byte slots**. A slot holds one wasm value,
39	little-endian, in its low bytes: i32/f32 in bytes 0..3 (f32 as its IEEE bit
40	pattern), i64/f64 in bytes 0..7, v128 in bytes 0..15 (byte *i* is lane byte
41	*i*). Unused bytes are don't-care on input and may be anything on output. Slot
42	arrays are 16-byte aligned.
43	
44	Names are encoded as **lowercase hex of their raw UTF-8 bytes**. For example
45	`add` → `616464`, the empty name → `` (empty string).
46	
47	## Symbols the generated module must define (external linkage)
48	
49	| symbol | signature | meaning |
50	|---|---|---|
51	| `w2l_init` | `void ()` | Instantiate: allocate memory and table, initialize globals, apply active element/data segments, run the start function. Called exactly once, before anything else. May trap. |
52	| `w2l_export_<hex(name)>` | `void (ptr args, ptr results)` | One per **exported function**. `args` holds the parameters (slot *i* = parameter *i*); write result *i* into `results` slot *i*. |
53	| `w2l_global_<hex(name)>` | `void (ptr out)` | One per **exported global**: write its current value into slot `out`. |
54	| `w2l_memory_<hex(name)>` | `ptr (ptr size_out)` | One per **exported memory**: return the base address of linear memory and store its current size in bytes (i64) to `*size_out`. |
55	
56	Exported tables need no symbol.
57	
58	## Symbols the harness provides
59	
60	| symbol | signature | meaning |
61	|---|---|---|
62	| `w2l_trap` | `void (i32 code)` **noreturn** | Report a trap. It never returns (the harness `longjmp`s out of your code). |
63	| `w2l_import_<hex(module)>_<hex(name)>` | `void (ptr args, ptr results)` | One per imported function, same slot convention as exports. |
64	
65	The harness provides these host functions for import:
66	
67	| module | name | type | effect |
68	|---|---|---|---|
69	| `spectest` | `print`, `print_i32`, `print_i64`, `print_f32`, `print_f64`, `print_i32_f32`, `print_f64_f64` | params as named, no results | write to the host output |
70	| `env` | `print_i32` (i32), `print_i64` (i64), `print_f32` (f32), `print_f64` (f64), `print_v128` (v128), `putchar` (i32) | no results | write to the host output |
71	
72	A module importing anything else may fail to load. That is not your problem.
73	
74	## Trap codes
75	
76	When execution traps, call `w2l_trap` with:
77	
78	| code | trap |
79	|---|---|
80	| 0 | `unreachable` executed |
81	| 1 | integer divide by zero |
82	| 2 | integer overflow (`INT_MIN / -1`, trapping float→int out of range) |
83	| 3 | invalid conversion to integer (trapping float→int of NaN) |
84	| 4 | out-of-bounds memory access, including `memory.init/copy/fill` and data segments |
85	| 5 | out-of-bounds table access / undefined element, including `call_indirect` index ≥ table size, `table.init/copy` and element segments |
86	| 6 | uninitialized element (`call_indirect` to a null entry) |
87	| 7 | indirect call type mismatch |
88	| 8 | call stack exhausted |
89	
90	The test harness checks the exact code.
91	
92	## Call stack exhaustion
93	
94	Unbounded recursion must trap with code 8 in bounded time, never hang or crash.
95	The harness runs wasm code on a thread with an 8 MiB stack and a large guard
96	region below it; a native stack overflow that faults inside that guard region is
97	reported as trap 8. Legitimate recursion at least 10 000 frames deep (small
98	frames) must work.
99	
100	## Instance state after a trap
101	
102	After a trap the harness may call further exports of the same instance. That is
103	legal wasm, since a trap does not destroy the instance. Make sure no internal
104	bookkeeping (such as a depth counter) is left corrupted when `w2l_trap` unwinds
105	your code.
106	
107	## Memory
108	
109	Linear memory starts at its declared minimum size and grows with `memory.grow`
110	up to its declared maximum, or 65536 pages if there is none. `memory.grow` returns -1
111	if growth exceeds the limit (or cannot be satisfied). Otherwise it returns the old
112	size in pages, and the new pages are zeroed. The address returned by
113	`w2l_memory_*` is only required to be valid until the next call into the module.
114	
115	A worked, hand-written example of the ABI is in `examples/abi/`
116	(`example.wat` and its translation `example.ll`).

| 6 | uninitialized element (`call_indirect` to a null entry) |
| 7 | indirect call type mismatch |
| 8 | call stack exhausted |

The test harness checks the exact code.

## Call stack exhaustion

Unbounded recursion must trap with code 8 in bounded time, never hang or crash.
The harness runs wasm code on a thread with an 8 MiB stack and a large guard
region below it; a native stack overflow that faults inside that guard region is
reported as trap 8. Legitimate recursion at least 10 000 frames deep (small
frames) must work.

## Instance state after a trap

After a trap the harness may call further exports of the same instance. That is
legal wasm, since a trap does not destroy the instance. Make sure no internal
bookkeeping (such as a depth counter) is left corrupted when `w2l_trap` unwinds
your code.

## Memory

Linear memory starts at its declared minimum size and grows with `memory.grow`
up to its declared maximum, or 65536 pages if there is none. `memory.grow` returns -1
if growth exceeds the limit (or cannot be satisfied). Otherwise it returns the old
size in pages, and the new pages are zeroed. The address returned by
`w2l_memory_*` is only required to be valid until the next call into the module.

A worked, hand-written example of the ABI is in `examples/abi/`
(`example.wat` and its translation `example.ll`).

## Read-only inventory

All four `.wasm` files passed `wasm-tools validate`. They have version-1 headers, but that does **not** mean they use MVP-only features. The payload contract at `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/payloads/README.md` explicitly requires full support for every proposal found, beyond the instructions exercised here.

### Proposals and observed scope

- **Multi-value** — `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/payloads/multi-value/multi-value.wasm`  
  Its type section includes functions returning two `i32`s. `swap` and `sum_diff` return pairs; `block_pair` uses a block with two results; `block_param` uses a block with two `i32` parameters and one result. This requires multi-result function types and type-indexed block types with parameters/results. Full support means arbitrary result arities and multi-value semantics for `block`, `loop`, and `if`—not just these pair-return examples. It adds no new opcode.

- **Fixed 128-bit SIMD** — `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/payloads/minicelt/minicelt.wasm`, `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/payloads/minisilk/minisilk.wasm`, and `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/payloads/qoa-simd/qoa-simd.wasm`  
  The feature adds the `v128` type and `0xfd`-prefixed operators. The following is the **union of SIMD mnemonics actually present**:

  - `v128`: `and`, `any_true`, `bitselect`, `const`, `load`, `load8_splat`, `load16_splat`, `load32_splat`, `load16x4_s`, `load32_zero`, `load64_zero`, `load8_lane`, `load16_lane`, `load32_lane`, `not`, `or`, `store`, `store32_lane`, `store64_lane`, `xor`.
  - `i8x16`: `abs`, `shuffle`, `swizzle`.
  - `i16x8`: `add`, `sub`, `shr_s`, `extract_lane_s`, `extract_lane_u`, `narrow_i32x4_s`, `narrow_i32x4_u`, `extend_low_i8x16_s`, `extend_low_i8x16_u`, `extend_high_i8x16_s`.
  - `i32x4`: `abs`, `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `neg`, `eq`, `ne`, `lt_s`, `gt_s`, `min_s`, `min_u`, `max_s`, `shl`, `shr_s`, `shr_u`, `splat`, `extract_lane`, `replace_lane`, `bitmask`, `dot_i16x8_s`, `extend_low_i16x8_s`, `extend_low_i16x8_u`, `extend_high_i16x8_s`, `extmul_low_i16x8_s`, `extmul_high_i16x8_s`, `trunc_sat_f32x4_s`, `trunc_sat_f32x4_u`.
  - `i64x2`: `add`, `mul`, `shl`, `shr_s`, `shr_u`, `all_true`, `extract_lane`, `gt_s`, `lt_s`, `splat`, `extend_low_i32x4_s`, `extend_low_i32x4_u`, `extend_high_i32x4_s`, `extend_high_i32x4_u`, `extmul_low_i32x4_s`, `extmul_high_i32x4_s`.
  - `f32x4`: `abs`, `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `neg`, `floor`, `eq`, `lt`, `gt`, `extract_lane`, `replace_lane`, `splat`, `pmin`, `pmax`, `convert_i32x4_s`, `demote_f64x2_zero`.
  - `f64x2`: `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `extract_lane`, `splat`, `convert_low_i32x4_s`, `promote_low_f32x4`.

  Distinguishing evidence: CELT uses `f32x4.pmin/pmax` and vector saturating conversions; SILK uses `i32x4.dot_i16x8_s`, `i16x8.narrow_i32x4_*`, and `v128.load16x4_s`; QOA uses `i64x2.all_true`, `i64x2.extmul_*_i32x4_s`, and `v128.store64_lane`. The README’s full-proposal requirement means supporting the complete fixed SIMD proposal, not just this union; no relaxed-SIMD operators were observed.

- **Non-trapping float-to-int conversion** — CELT, SILK, and QOA audio binaries  
  Scalar forms observed: `i32.trunc_sat_f32_s`, `i32.trunc_sat_f64_s`, and `i32.trunc_sat_f64_u`. They use the `0xfc` prefix with subopcodes `0x00`, `0x02`, and `0x03`. Full proposal support requires all eight scalar forms: `i32` and `i64` destinations, `f32` and `f64` sources, signed and unsigned. The vector forms `i32x4.trunc_sat_f32x4_s/u` are SIMD operators, not these scalar forms.

- **Sign-extension operators** — CELT, SILK, and QOA audio binaries  
  Observed: `i32.extend16_s` (all three), `i32.extend8_s` (SILK), and `i64.extend16_s` (SILK), using opcodes `0xc1`, `0xc0`, and `0xc3`. Full support requires all five opcodes `0xc0`–`0xc4`: also `i64.extend8_s` and `i64.extend32_s`.

- **Bulk memory operations** — CELT and SILK use `memory.copy` and `memory.fill`; QOA uses `memory.fill`. These share the `0xfc` prefix (`0x0a` and `0x0b`). CELT and SILK also contain a **DataCount** section (section id 12; data-segment vectors have 8 and 2 entries respectively), though no `memory.init` or `data.drop` instruction appears, and the displayed data segments are active. Full bulk-memory support extends beyond the observed operations to `memory.init`, `data.drop`, `table.init`, `elem.drop`, and `table.copy`, including passive segment handling and DataCount validation. No table/element section or reference-type operator appears in these payloads; the bundled bulk-memory overview attributes `table.grow`/`table.fill` to reference types.

- **Branch-hint metadata** — QOA only  
  `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/payloads/qoa-simd/qoa-simd.wasm` contains `custom "metadata.code.branch_hint"`: WABT reports 31 code-offset hints across functions 4–7, with hint bytes `0` or `1`. This is custom metadata, not an executable instruction or value type; a translator can ignore it for execution semantics, but must not reject the payload because of it.

### Sections and types

`minicelt.wasm` and `minisilk.wasm` have Type, Function, Memory, Global, Export, DataCount, Code, and Data sections. `multi-value.wasm` has Type, Function, Memory, Export, and Code. `qoa-simd.wasm` has Type, Function, Memory, Global, Export, Start, Code, Data, and the branch-hint custom section. There are **no imports, tables, or element sections** in these modules. Audio modules start with two memory pages; the multi-value example starts with one. Data segments are active.

The SIMD binaries use `v128` in code; the CELT type section also contains an internal `(param i32 v128)` signature. The multi-value example’s multi-result/block-parameter forms are visible in its type and code sections. Standard scalar/control/memory operations (`i32`, `i64`, `f32`, `f64`, loads/stores, branches, calls, locals and globals) are also used.

### ABI gotchas

- The payload READMEs specify no Wasm imports. CELT and SILK have no start function: call their `*_init` export after instantiation. QOA has a start function, which the ABI’s `w2l_init` must run before exports; then call `encode_init`.
- The generated-code contract in `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/ABI.md` passes values in **16-byte slots**. Multi-value results occupy successive result slots, in order. Exported `i32` pointers are Wasm linear-memory byte offsets, not native pointers.
- CELT accepts 1 or 2 channels and `960 * channels` samples. Its f32 and i16 input-pointer exports alias the same buffer, which the encoder mutates; rewrite it before every call. SILK is mono and accepts 320 samples. Both return a packet length/error and use an output buffer documented as 1276 bytes.
- QOA accepts 1–31 channels and `frameLen <= 5120`; the driver supplies `frameLen * channels` interleaved i16 samples. Its README’s reference driver places input at `heap_base`, output at the next 16-byte-aligned address, and may need to grow memory. `decode_frame` updates the exported mutable `frame_channels`, `frame_samplerate`, and `frame_samples` globals. The initial memory is two pages; `heap_base` is 65536.
- The ABI says a returned memory base need only remain valid until the next module call, so reacquire it after calls that may grow memory.

Evidence includes `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/payloads/README.md`, the four payload READMEs and binaries, and `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/ABI.md`. The referenced proposal notes are under `/mnt/workspace/w2l-runs/runv2_gpt6_luna/docs/wasm-proposals/`.
